\chapter{Telling Time}
\label{ch:la-telling-time}
\hlchaptermodality{13}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can talk about the hour in Latin, and explain why a Roman hour was not a fixed sixty minutes.}

Say hōra, then work out how long a Roman hour actually was on a winter day against a summer one.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hōra]{hōra — the source word, and an hour that wasn't always 60 minutes}

\label{lesson:LA-C13-hora}



\begin{quote}
You already met \textbf{nōna hōra}, \textquotedblleft{}the ninth hour,\textquotedblright{} in an earlier lesson — now meet the word itself, and an honest surprise about what a Roman \textquotedblleft{}hour\textquotedblright{} actually was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: hōra $\leftarrow$ Greek h\'{\={o}}rā}
\textbf{hōra} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{hour}\textquotedblright{} — borrowed from \textbf{Greek} \textbf{h\'{\={o}}rā}, \textquotedblleft{}a season, the right time, a time of day\textquotedblright{} (the Greek goddesses of the seasons, the \emph{Hōrai}, share this root). Latin narrowed the broader Greek sense down to today's specific meaning: one twelfth of the day.

\begin{culture}
Here's the part that trips people up: the Romans divided \textbf{daylight} — sunrise to sunset — into \textbf{12 equal hōrae}, and \textbf{night} into another 12. But since daylight itself is longer in summer and shorter in winter, \textbf{each hōra stretched or shrank with the seasons}: a summer daytime hōra in Rome could run close to 75 modern minutes, a winter one closer to 45. Only at the two equinoxes did an hōra land close to today's fixed 60 minutes. This is exactly why \textbf{nōna hōra} (\textquotedblleft{}the ninth hour,\textquotedblright{} counted from sunrise) landed around 3 p.m. at the equinox but could shift earlier or later depending on the season — and why it drifted, over centuries, into the fixed clock-time we call \textquotedblleft{}noon.\textquotedblright{}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hōra\textquotedblright{} — the source word, Greek \emph{h\'{\={o}}rā} underneath
  \item the honest surprise — a Roman hōra stretched and shrank with the seasons, it wasn't a fixed 60 minutes
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hōra / hora / heure / hour\textquotedblright{} — one root, four different fates
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Greek word is \emph{hōra} from, and what did it originally mean? (\emph{h\'{\={o}}rā} — \textquotedblleft{}a season, the right time.\textquotedblright{}) Was a Roman hōra always 60 minutes long? (\textbf{No} — it was 1/12 of that day's actual daylight or nighttime span, so it stretched in summer and shrank in winter.) Which of Spanish, French, and German did \textbf{not} directly inherit this word from Latin? (\textbf{German} — it borrowed \emph{Uhr} separately, much later.)
\end{tcolorbox}
